interface CanonicalPayload { statement: string; studentResponse: string; creditedAnswers: string[]; explanation?: string; category?: string; coach?: { drill: string; rubric: string[]; partial_rule?: string }; ideas?: unknown; attemptNo: number }
interface Receipt { ok: boolean; status: string; httpStatus?: number; code?: string; retryAfterSeconds?: number; claimId?: string; payload?: CanonicalPayload; result?: unknown }
export type ReceiptRpc = (name: string, args: Record<string, unknown>) => Promise<Receipt>;
export interface GradeReply { body: unknown; status: number }
function reply(body: unknown, status = 200): GradeReply { return { body, status }; }
function receiptReply(receipt: Receipt): GradeReply {
  const status = Number.isInteger(receipt.httpStatus) && receipt.httpStatus! >= 400 && receipt.httpStatus! <= 599 ? receipt.httpStatus! : 503;
  return reply({ error: "The judgment could not be confirmed.", code: receipt.code ?? "unavailable", retryAfter: receipt.retryAfterSeconds }, status);
}
/** One numbered thing the caller wants judged for coverage, not just credit. */
interface Idea {
  n: number;
  text: string;
}

/**
 * Callers that ask for coverage send a numbered checklist. Anything malformed
 * drops the whole request for coverage rather than half-asking for it, since a
 * partial checklist would read to the student as "these are all the ideas".
 */
function readIdeas(raw: unknown): Idea[] | null {
  if (!Array.isArray(raw) || !raw.length) return null;
  const ideas: Idea[] = [];
  for (const item of raw) {
    const n = Number(item?.n);
    const text = item?.text;
    if (!Number.isInteger(n) || typeof text !== "string" || !text.trim()) return null;
    ideas.push({ n, text: text.trim() });
  }
  return ideas;
}

    // answer box, so without this they play behind the student while they are
    // still looking at what they typed. Desktop already has both in view.
    if (typeof window === "undefined" || window.matchMedia("(min-width: 768px)").matches) return;

import { cn } from "@/lib/utils";
import type { ActivityItem, FeedbackState } from "../api/types";

interface CoachFeedbackProps {
  verdict: FeedbackState;
  feedback: string;
  /** When true, show the credited answer. Only a reveal earns that. */
  revealed: boolean;
  /**
   * When true, the item is finished one way or another. The authored
   * explanation shows from here on, including on a correct answer: it names the
   * indicator word and the discrimination the item teaches, and withholding it
   * from the students who are getting it right is backwards.
   */
  resolved: boolean;
  /**
   * What to call the credited answers after the first. Authored per Activity,
   * because the generic wording is wrong wherever the second answer is not an
   * alternative phrasing: in Conditional Rephrase it is the contrapositive, the
   * other half of what the task asked for.
   */
  secondaryLabel?: string;
  item: ActivityItem;
}

const DEFAULT_SECONDARY_LABEL = "Also accepted";

const VERDICT_STYLE: Record<FeedbackState, { label: string; chip: string; dot: string }> = {
  correct: {
    label: "Correct",
    chip: "bg-[hsl(var(--state-correct)/0.12)] text-[hsl(var(--ac-emerald-strong))]",
    dot: "bg-[hsl(var(--state-correct))]",
  },
  partial: {
    label: "Almost",
    chip: "bg-[hsl(var(--state-warn)/0.14)] text-[hsl(38_92%_34%)]",
    dot: "bg-[hsl(var(--state-warn))]",
  },
  incorrect: {
    label: "Not yet",
    chip: "bg-[hsl(var(--state-incorrect)/0.12)] text-[hsl(350_80%_45%)]",
    dot: "bg-[hsl(var(--state-incorrect))]",
  },
  // Deliberately neutral. The student answered and nobody read it; the app has
  // no basis for the red chip it used to show here.
  unchecked: {
    label: "Not checked",
    chip: "bg-[hsl(var(--muted))] text-muted-foreground",
    dot: "bg-[hsl(var(--muted-foreground)/0.6)]",
  },
};

/** Coach verdict chip + message, the authored teaching note, and the reveal. */
export function CoachFeedback({
  verdict,
  feedback,
  revealed,
  resolved,
  secondaryLabel,
  item,
}: CoachFeedbackProps) {
  const style = VERDICT_STYLE[verdict];
  return (
    <div className="space-y-4">
      <div className="flex items-center gap-2">
        <span
          className={cn(
            "inline-flex items-center gap-1.5 rounded-full px-3 py-1 text-xs font-semibold",
            style.chip,
          )}
        >
          <span className={cn("h-1.5 w-1.5 rounded-full", style.dot)} />
          {style.label}
        </span>
      </div>

      {feedback && <p className="text-[15px] leading-relaxed text-foreground/85">{feedback}</p>}

      {revealed && (
        <div className="rounded-2xl border border-border bg-[hsl(var(--muted)/0.5)] p-4">
          <p className="text-xs font-medium uppercase tracking-wide text-muted-foreground">
            Credited answer
          </p>
          <p className="mt-1.5 text-[15px] font-medium text-foreground">
            {item.credited_answers[0]}
          </p>
          {item.credited_answers.length > 1 && (
            <p className="mt-1 text-xs text-muted-foreground">
              {secondaryLabel || DEFAULT_SECONDARY_LABEL}: {item.credited_answers.slice(1).join(" · ")}
            </p>
          )}
        </div>
      )}

      {resolved && item.explanation && (
        <p className="border-l-2 border-[hsl(var(--ac-emerald)/0.35)] pl-4 text-sm leading-relaxed text-foreground/75">
          {item.explanation}
        </p>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}

/* ---------- The field ---------- */

/* Each word sits on the baseline grid with a star-point under it. The word
   gap is an explicit margin: an inline-block trims its own trailing space, so
   without this the whole statement sets as one unbroken string. */
.ob-word {
  position: relative;
  display: inline-block;
  padding-bottom: 10px;
  margin-right: 0.34em;
}

.ob-word::after {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  left: 50%;
  bottom: 2px;
  width: 2px;
  height: 2px;
  border-radius: 50%;
  background: hsl(var(--ob-star) / 0.45);
  transform: translateX(-50%);
}

/* An indicator's star flares once its figure is drawn, and not before:
   lighting it early would answer the question. */
.ob-word[data-anchor="true"][data-drawn="true"]::after {
  width: 5px;
  height: 5px;
  background: hsl(var(--ob-star));
  box-shadow:
    0 0 8px hsl(var(--ob-star)),
    0 0 22px hsl(var(--ob-star) / 0.6);
}

/* The four-point glint over a drawn anchor star. */
.ob-word[data-anchor="true"][data-drawn="true"]::before {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  left: 50%;
  bottom: -2.5px;
  width: 11px;
  height: 11px;
  transform: translateX(-50%);
  background:
    linear-gradient(0deg, transparent 46%, hsl(var(--ob-star) / 0.9) 50%, transparent 54%),
    linear-gradient(90deg, transparent 46%, hsl(var(--ob-star) / 0.9) 50%, transparent 54%);
}

.ob-word[data-anchor="true"][data-drawn="true"] {
  color: hsl(var(--ob-ink));
  text-shadow: 0 0 14px hsl(var(--ob-star) / 0.5);
}

@keyframes ob-shimmer {
  0%,
  100% {
    opacity: 0.4;
  }
  50% {
    opacity: 1;
  }
}

/* The arrival shimmer: once, then still. */
.ob-field[data-arriving="true"] .ob-word::after {
  animation: ob-shimmer 200ms ease-in-out 1;
}

/* ---------- The three geometries ---------- */

.ob-figure {
  fill: none;
  stroke: hsl(var(--ob-line));
  stroke-linecap: round;
}

/* Conditional: a single hard, precise shaft, drawn in gold. A rule. */
.ob-figure[data-kind="conditional"] {
  stroke: hsl(var(--ob-cond));
  stroke-width: 1.75;
  filter: drop-shadow(0 0 6px hsl(var(--ob-cond) / 0.85));
}

/* Causal: doubled and heavier, in comet cyan. Something pushes. */
.ob-figure[data-kind="causal"] {
  stroke: hsl(var(--ob-caus));
  stroke-width: 2.5;
  filter: drop-shadow(0 0 7px hsl(var(--ob-caus) / 0.85));
}

/* Comparative: the beam, in nebula rose. Weight, not direction. */
.ob-figure[data-kind="comparative"] {
  stroke: hsl(var(--ob-comp));
  stroke-width: 2;
  filter: drop-shadow(0 0 6px hsl(var(--ob-comp) / 0.85));
}

.ob-arrowhead {
  fill: hsl(var(--ob-line));
  stroke: none;

g[data-kind="conditional"] .ob-arrowhead {
  fill: hsl(var(--ob-cond));
}

g[data-kind="causal"] .ob-arrowhead {
  fill: hsl(var(--ob-caus));
}

/* Drawn on verdict over 420ms. The dash length is set inline from the measured

.ob-figure[data-draw="true"] {
  animation: ob-draw 420ms cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1) both;
}

@keyframes ob-draw {
  from {
    stroke-dashoffset: var(--ob-len, 200);

  to {
    stroke-dashoffset: 0;
  }
}

/* A wrongly named relationship: the shape is visibly tried, then dissolves. */
.ob-figure[data-ghost="true"] {

@keyframes ob-dissolve {
  0% {
    opacity: 0.7;

    opacity: 0.5;
  }
  100% {

  }

.ob-beam {

    const lift = Math.max(3, Math.min(10, seg.room - 9));
    const d = `M ${seg.x1} ${base} Q ${(seg.x1 + seg.x2) / 2} ${base - 2 * lift} ${seg.x2} ${base}`;
    return { seg, base, lift, d, len: Math.ceil(seg.x2 - seg.x1 + 4 * lift + 24) };
  });

  const direction = kind === "conditional" ? directionOf(indicators[0]) : null;
  const first = shapes[0];
  const last = shapes[shapes.length - 1];
  const head =
    direction === "necessary"
      ? { x: first.seg.x1, y: first.base }
      : { x: last.seg.x2, y: last.base };
  const showHead = kind === "causal" || (kind === "conditional" && direction !== null);

  return (
    <g data-testid={`ob-figure-${kind}`} data-kind={kind}>
      {shapes.map(({ d, len }, n) => (
        <path
          key={n}
          className="ob-figure"
          data-kind={kind}
          data-draw={still ? undefined : "true"}
          d={d}
          style={
            still
              ? undefined
              : ({ strokeDasharray: len, ["--ob-len" as string]: len } as React.CSSProperties)
          }
        />
      ))}
      {/* Causal is doubled: a second shaft just above the first, so the push is
          visible in the line's weight rather than in a colour. Above, not
          below: below is where the letters are. */}
      {kind === "causal"
        ? shapes.map(({ d }, n) => (
            <path
              key={`echo-${n}`}
              className="ob-figure"
              data-kind="causal"
              d={d}
              transform="translate(0,-3)"
              opacity={0.6}
            />
          ))
        : null}
      {/* Comparative gets a level beam under each stretch that spans two terms.
          Level, because the figure does not know which term is greater, and an
          "as strong as" has no greater term at all. */}
      {kind === "comparative"
        ? shapes
            .filter(({ seg }) => seg.count > 1)
            .map(({ seg, base }, n) => (
              <g key={`beam-${n}`} className="ob-beam" data-testid="ob-beam">
                <line
                  className="ob-figure"
                  data-kind="comparative"
                  x1={seg.x1}
                  y1={base}
                  x2={seg.x2}
                  y2={base}
                />
              </g>
            ))
        : null}
      {showHead ? (
        <polygon
          className="ob-arrowhead"
          data-testid={`ob-head-${kind}`}
          points={`${head.x},${head.y} ${head.x - 4},${head.y - 7} ${head.x + 4},${head.y - 7}`}
        />
      ) : null}
    </g>
  );
}

'''+s[end:]

# Copy corrections

Every student-facing wording fix, with the reason it was wrong. Read this before
writing or editing copy for LSAT U so the same mistake is not made twice.

Companion to [[teaching-voice]], which says how the writing should sound. This
says what has actually gone wrong and why.

Started 2026-09-07 from a Read, Recall, Colour pass. Add to it every time a
correction is made.

## The rules these corrections came from

Three rules already existed and all three leaked anyway, because each was
enforced on the components that happened to exist when it was written. A surface
added later starts uncovered.

- **No em dashes, ever.** [[teaching-voice]], Core voice.
- **No internal vocabulary in student copy.** `projects/lsatu/src/features/activity-centre/CONTEXT.md`
  carries the glossary and marks what to avoid.
- **Every CSS token a stylesheet uses must be defined in it.** `projects/lsatu/CLAUDE.md`.

Guards now live with the content rather than with each component:
`content/instructions-voice.test.ts` checks the authored instructions, so every
surface that renders them is covered, including surfaces not written yet.

## Corrections

### Contrapositive and arrow lessons: cut the sophistry (2026-10-11)

Joshua rejected the first contrapositive lesson as 'terribly done' and then rejected the rewrite for 'a lot of sophistry'. Rules from the two rounds:

- **Say what it is first, in plain words, before any example.** Name the idea, say what it states, then show it. The contrapositive is the **same rule said a different way**. The two are **logically equivalent**: if one is true, the other is true, and you can use either. Lead with that. Source: his 
- **No metaphor-of-obligation language.** Never write that a rule 'makes a promise', that the left side 'depends on' the right, or that it has 'nothing to stand on'. Say what is true and why, in the plainest reasoning: if the left side had happened, the right side would have come with it.
- **Keep it natural, intuitive and personable.** Contractions, short sentences, a teacher thinking next to the student. No lecture-hall phrasing. If a sentence sounds like it is trying to sound wise, cut it.
- **Name the lesson by its topic.** 'Contrapositive', not 'Write and read the contrapositive'.
- **A lesson explains before it drills.** Order for a concept lesson: what it is, see it work, how to do it, what it is not, the steps in short, why it matters. Do not open with an example or a question.
- **Must arrow note must say:** what the arrow says, where to start reading (the left), and what the arrow is for. Not just which side is sufficient.
- **A card front asks the question, the back gives the answer first.** The answer is the large line. Be specific: 'Can you read a rule from right to left?', not 'Can you reverse the arrow?'. Never 'the other one'.
- **Fix the vague word, not the sentence.** 'Reverse' and 'the other one' were both rejected as not specific. Say what the student actually does or what the condition actually is.
- **Never call the contrapositive 'the one other thing' a rule tells you.** Joshua (2026-10-11): it is not the only other thing you know. Say the two are equivalent and interchangeable: know one, you know the other. Do not claim a closed list of what else is known.
- **Do not use the raffle (win the raffle, get a bicycle) as the example in new contrapositive or arrow material.** Pick a fresh everyday example for each lesson. The contrapositive note now uses an elevator: if it is moving, its doors are closed. The older course text still uses the raffle; replace
- **Contrapositive lesson (Joshua, 2026-10-11, final): no thought experiment, no guess box, no flip card.** An earlier coat-and-guess card confused him ('I don't know what you did about that coat example'). Follow the source HTML's explanation of the contrapositive directly, in close language, impro

## Conditional Rephrase: name the student action, not the internal model (2026-09-15)

**Cut:** “record the route,” “choose the route,” and a map presented as five rules.

**Keep:** diagram the statement on paper, choose the matching diagram, and organize
the map into four groups. “Required means right” is a separate takeaway because it
explains placement; it is not a fifth group.

“Route” described the system’s representation, not the student’s work. Calling five
unlike ideas rules also flattened the teaching structure and made the layout harder to
read.

**Lesson:** name the action the student can see herself doing. Do not force a teaching
reminder into the same hierarchy as the categories it explains.

Related: [[teaching-voice]] · [[ASSIGN-AN-ACTIVITY]] · [[STUDENT-PLATFORM-IDENTITY-MAP]]

import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";
import { CoachFeedback } from "./CoachFeedback";
import type { ActivityItem } from "../api/types";

// Two things a student could not see before. The authored explanation names the
// indicator word and the discrimination the item teaches, and it was gated
// behind the reveal -- so the students who answered correctly, and only them,
// never read a word of the drill's own teaching. And the contrapositive, which
// the task asks for by name, was labelled as optional extra credit.

const item: ActivityItem = {
  order: 1,
  prompt: "Whenever the greenhouse fans run overnight, the orchids bloom by morning.",
  credited_answers: [
    "If the fans run overnight, then the orchids bloom by morning.",
    "If the orchids did not bloom by morning, then the fans did not run overnight.",
  ],
  explanation: '"Whenever" (sufficient). "Whenever," like "every" and "all," marks the sufficient side.',
};

const EXPLANATION = /marks the sufficient side/;

function show(props: Partial<React.ComponentProps<typeof CoachFeedback>> = {}) {
  render(
    <CoachFeedback
      verdict="correct"
      feedback=""
      revealed={false}
      resolved={false}
      item={item}
      {...props}
    />,
  );
}

describe("the teaching a resolved item shows", () => {
  it("shows the authored explanation on a correct answer, with no reveal", () => {
    show({ verdict: "correct", resolved: true, revealed: false });
    expect(screen.getByText(EXPLANATION)).toBeInTheDocument();
    show({ resolved: true, revealed: true, item: { ...item, credited_answers: [item.credited_answers[0]] } });
    expect(screen.queryByText(/Also accepted:/)).not.toBeInTheDocument();
    expect(screen.queryByText(/Contrapositive:/)).not.toBeInTheDocument();
  });
});

Fix Spot the Relationship: figures, answer reading, and leaked notes

The Observatory drew figures through the words of the line above. Marks
were placed from the word's span box (which includes half-leading) less a
fixed offset, and md:text-2xl silently replaced leading-loose with a 32px
line height, leaving 6px between lines. Figures now measure glyph boxes,
split per line, and stay inside the measured gap; the field has real
leading at every width. The comparative beam no longer rotates around the
whole field, and no longer tips toward a "greater" side it cannot know.

The answer reader missed "comparison" (the drill's own dial label),
"causation", "necessary condition" and "if-then", and counted a type the
student ruled out ("not causal") as a claim. A correct Coach verdict now
always draws the whole figure, so "Correct" never sits over "Still
undrawn".

Explanations render *emphasis* instead of asterisks (all Activities).

Content: removes production notes students could read ("his heater seed",
"Pair A, conditional half", "the Coach names the ambiguity"), a teaching
note pasted into item 40's answer key, item 40's wrong relationship
count, full stops inside quoted indicators, and "statement" in student
copy. The live database still holds the old content; this commit changes
the repo file only.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

## What was wrong

- **Figures drawn through the text.** Any figure on line 2 or lower was drawn across the line above it (item 29's causal mark struck through "lower than eight percent"). Two causes: marks were placed from the span box, which includes half-leading, and `md:text-2xl` overrode `leading-loose` with a 32px line height, leaving 6px between lines.
- **Comparative beam off its words.** SVG `transform-origin: center` rotated the beam around the whole field, and it tipped toward a "greater" side even on "as strong as".
- **Answer reader disagreed with the Coach.** "comparison, louder than" (the dial's own label) read as missing the comparative; "causation", "necessary condition", "if-then" failed the same way; "requires (not causal)" drew a ghost causal figure. The stage never saw the verdict, so "Correct" could sit over "Still undrawn".
- **Asterisks shown to students.** Explanations printed `*makes*` raw (affects every Activity that uses emphasis).
- **Production notes in student copy.** "matching his heater seed", "Pair A, conditional half", "the Coach names the ambiguity", "in the bank"; item 40 had a teaching note inside its answer key and declared 4 relationships while listing 3; seven answer keys had full stops inside the quoted indicator.

## What changed

- Line-aware figures measured from glyph boxes, one stretch per line, kept inside the measured gap; real leading at every width.
- Level beam with `transform-box: fill-box`.
- Wider type vocabulary and negation handling in `readAnswer`; the world now receives the verdict and draws the full figure on a correct answer.
- `CoachFeedback` renders explanations through `renderInlineMarks`.
- Content fixes in `spot-the-relationship.json`. **The live `activities` row is unchanged**; pushing content to the database is a separate step.

I fixed most of Spot the Relationship's problems, but **none of it is live yet**. The fixes are in [PR #207](https://github.com/vnjkoxpl-42905/lsatu-684d89db/pull/207), which isn't merged. The live database still holds the old content, so students see the old version until that's pushed.

## Why it wasn't working properly

**1. The drawings cut through the sentence.** After you answer, the activity draws a mark over the key words. Any mark on the second line or lower was drawn across the line above it. On item 29, the "because … expands" mark struck straight through "lower than eight percent". The root cause was a styling setting that squeezed the lines to 6px apart at desktop width, so nothing could fit between them.

**2. The drawing and the grading could contradict each other.** Two separate things judge each answer: an AI Coach decides right or wrong, and a simple word-matcher decides what to draw. They never talked. So:
- "comparison, louder than" showed "Still undrawn: comparative", because the matcher only knew the word "comparative". The activity's own button says "Comparison".
- "causation", "necessary condition" and "if-then" failed the same way.
- "conditional, requires (not causal)" drew a fake causal mark for the exact mistake the student had just avoided.
- A student could get a green "Correct" with "Still undrawn" underneath.

**3. Your production notes were showing to students.** After each question, students read things like "matching his heater seed", "Pair A, conditional half" and "the Coach names the ambiguity rather than letting a rule form". Item 40 had a teaching note pasted into its answer key and claimed 4 relationships while listing 3. Seven answer keys had a full stop inside the quotes ("lags.").

**4. Students saw literal asterisks** like `*makes*` in explanations. This also affected Spot the Callback, Vocab Rehab and Rebuttal Rephrase.

**5. Smaller problems.** The comparison beam rotated around the middle of the whole box instead of its own words. It also always tipped one way, even on "as strong as". And the three dials (Conditional / Causal / Comparison) never light up in the real activity, because nothing feeds them.

## What I fixed

- Each mark now sits over its own words on its own line. I checked this in the browser at desktop and phone width on items 29 and 47.
- The grading result drives the drawing, so a correct answer always shows the full picture. The matcher now knows the common names for each type and ignores a type the student ruled out.
- Explanations show italics instead of asterisks.
- I removed the production notes, fixed item 40 and the answer keys, and changed "statement" to "sentence" per your corrections log.
- I added tests for each bug. The 20 test failures in the suite also fail on untouched `main`, in other activities (mostly the Switchyard), so they're not from this change.

## What I didn't do

- **Pushed content to the live database.** It changes what an assigned student sees, so I'm waiting for your word. One student has it assigned and hasn't started; only the tester account has ever used it. Say "push the content" and I'll update the activity and that unstarted assignment, never completed work.
- **Tested the Coach live.** Every graded answer goes through Lovable's AI gateway and may spend credits, so I only reviewed its prompt in the code. Your notes were also being sent to the Coach as the "author's note", so it could repeat them in its feedback.
- **Fixed the dials.** They still never light.
- **Discarded a file the Lovable plugin rewrote** (`supabase/functions/mcp/index.ts`). The discard was blocked, so I left it out of the commit.

## How to improve it

1. **Grade exact answers instantly.** The answer keys are fully structured, so an answer naming every right type with a correct indicator word could be marked correct without the Coach. That's instant, free and consistent. Anything else would still go to the Coach. Conditional Rephrase already works this way. This is my top recommendation.
2. **Make the drawing teach direction.** Right now a conditional gets a small arc over "only if". It would teach more if it marked which part is required and which part is enough.
3. **Write real explanations for the hard items.** Most items from 33 to 48 just say "3 relationships in this sentence." Those need your voice.
4. **Settle one rule for you to decide.** Item 22 says "longer" and "deeper" aren't comparisons, and item 28 says "harder" isn't. But item 36 credits "longer", 31 credits "heavier", and 47 credits "higher still". Which way you go changes what students learn.
5. **Remove the "Rung 3" labels students see,** or rename them to something meaningful to a student.

I also added a `lsatu-str-dev` entry to the vault's `.claude/launch.json`. That dev server is still running on port 8095 if you want to look at `/activity-lab` → Observatory.

 *
 * The type is what gets matched; the indicator is checked separately, because
 * the drill's own rubric says type alone is not a complete answer and the
 * world should be able to show a figure drawn from the wrong anchor words.
 */
export function readAnswer(signal: Signal, response: string): Reading {
  const named = namedKinds(response);

  const real = new Set(signal.relations.map((r) => r.kind));

  const found = [...named].filter((k) => real.has(k));
  const invented = [...named].filter((k) => !real.has(k));
  const missed = [...real].filter((k) => !named.has(k));

  // Did they quote an actual indicator for each type they got right?
  const quotedIndicators =
    found.length > 0 &&
    found.every((kind) =>
      signal.relations
        .filter((r) => r.kind === kind)
        .some((r) =>
          r.indicators.some((ind) => {
            const bare = ind.replace(/[.,]+$/, "").split(/…|\.\.\./)[0].trim();
            return bare.length > 1 && new RegExp(`\\b${escape(bare)}\\b`, "i").test(response);
          }),
        ),
    );

  return { found, invented, missed, quotedIndicators, drawn: found };
}

/* ------------------------------------------------------------------ *
 * Instant grading
 * ------------------------------------------------------------------ */

/** Lowercase, straight quotes gone, "only-if" read as "only if". */
function normalize(text: string): string {
  return text
    .toLowerCase()
    .replace(/[‘’“”"'`]/g, " ")
    .replace(/[-_/]/g, " ")
    .replace(/\s+/g, " ");
}

/**
 * Words that turn a short indicator into a different one. "Only if" is not
 * "if", and a student who writes "only if" on an item keyed "if" has named the
 * wrong condition, so a bare "if" match inside "only if" proves nothing.
 */
const LONGER_FORM = /\b(?:only|even|as|not)\s+$/;

function quotes(indicator: string, answer: string): boolean {
  const parts = normalize(indicator.replace(/[.,]+$/, ""))
    .split(/…|\.\.\./)
    .map((p) => p.trim())
    .filter(Boolean);
  if (!parts.length) return false;
  return parts.every((part) => {
    const re = new RegExp(`\\b${escape(part)}\\b`, "g");
    for (const m of answer.matchAll(re)) {
      if (!LONGER_FORM.test(answer.slice(0, m.index))) return true;
    }
    return false;
  });
}

/**
 * True when an answer is the credited answer in substance: it names exactly the
 * types the sentence carries, none it does not, and quotes at least one
 * credited indicator for every relationship.
 *
 * This only ever says yes. False is not a verdict of wrong; it means the answer
 * needs judgment, and the Coach takes it. That is what makes it safe to trust:
 * it confirms the answer key rather than reasoning about the student.
 */
export function matchesCredited(item: ActivityItem, response: string): boolean {
  const signal = parseSignal(item);
  if (!signal || !response.trim()) return false;
  const named = namedKinds(response);
  const real = new Set(signal.relations.map((r) => r.kind));
  if (named.size !== real.size || [...named].some((k) => !real.has(k))) return false;
  const answer = normalize(response);
  return signal.relations.every((r) => r.indicators.some((ind) => quotes(ind, answer)));
}
EOF

1	---
2	name: lovable-frontend-publish-is-separate
3	description: A push builds a Lovable preview but never reaches lsatprep.study; publish with deploy_project, wait for the sync, and prove it from the bundle.
4	metadata:
5	  type: project
6	---
7	
8	Pushing to `main` makes Lovable build the commit — its project record shows a
9	preview screenshot tagged with the commit sha within minutes — but the published
10	site at lsatprep.study keeps serving the previous bundle until something calls
11	`deploy_project` (Lovable MCP, `project_id 53b9a6f2-aba7-4ae4-8dd1-fa5b8aab4d76`,
12	name `lsatu`). Confirmed 2026-09-08: a fix sat built-but-unpublished for 20
13	minutes with no error anywhere.
14	
15	**The sync lags the push.** `deploy_project` publishes whatever Lovable has
16	ingested, not what is on origin. On 2026-09-09 a deploy fired seconds after a
17	successful push and shipped the *previous* commit; `get_project` showed
18	`latest_commit_sha` catching up about three minutes later, and a second deploy
19	was needed. There is no error and no warning — the deploy reports `pending` and
20	succeeds, just on the wrong commit.
21	
22	**Why:** build, sync and publish are three separate steps, and none of them
23	reports that the others have not happened. A green push reads as shipped.
24	
25	**How to apply:** before calling `deploy_project`, call `get_project` and check
26	`latest_commit_sha` equals your HEAD; if it does not, wait and re-check. After
27	deploying, prove it from the bundle: pick a string **the commit alone**
28	introduces — not a class name an earlier deploy already shipped, which is how a
29	stale bundle passed a check on 2026-09-09 — then fetch `https://lsatprep.study/`,
30	read the `index-*` asset hash out of it, and grep the asset for the marker.
31	Allow several minutes; the hash changing is the signal a publish landed at all.
32	Note `deploy_project` ships every unpublished commit on main, not just yours.
33	
34	Same trap, different half: [[lovable-edge-functions-do-not-deploy-from-push]].
35	Related: [[push-only-your-own-commits]].
36	
37	**Standing permission (Joshua, 2026-09-26):** publishing the frontend with the
38	free `deploy_project` is pre-authorized, so he does not need to press Publish
39	himself. It applies only to that free path. Anything that spends or might spend
40	Lovable credits still needs his confirmation right before it runs
41	([[minimize-lovable-credits]]). If he opens Lovable after one of these publishes,
42	it will show nothing to publish, and that is expected.

## User Profile

Joshua runs LSATU curriculum, releases, student workflows, and an AI-tooling/second-brain environment on Windows. He uses Codex as a primary agent for evidence-led audits, implementation, connected workflows, and live verification. Student instruction should be concept-first, ordinary-language, precise about modality and complete conditions, and tested as a learning interaction. He is configuring Orca as a multi-agent workspace with Codex primary.

## User preferences

- Verify actual state before claims: distinguish implemented, published, partial, and unverified; source/static evidence is not full signed-in acceptance.
- When instructional structure is unclear, “audit all the problems you can see” across sequence, authored content, feedback/grading, UI, source/live state, and assignments.
- Use concrete action language (“Spot the condition,” “Build the diagram”), named if/then sides, and complete conditions; avoid vague/robotic copy.
- Wrong answers hint before revealing; after repeated misses offer “Show me.” Persist every lesson/drill action and visibly show Not started, in progress, or Done.
- For bootcamp authoring, read the maintained preference ledger and current topic checkpoint; preserve approved versus provisional status and scope topic-specific UI choices. [ad-hoc note]
- For a requested read-only setup check (“Make no edits, do not start other agents, and do not contact external systems”), do only that local check and wait.
- Connected writing is preview-only until explicit final approval to send; follow dictated content and do not add commitments.
- Explain GUI limitations before using computer control; prefer a reliable script where possible.

## General Tips

- Read C:\Users\Joshu\dev\ai-os\AGENTS.md before AI OS work: wiki/hot.md is fresh state; it requires high-confidence edits, one command per tool call, no automatic pickup, and explicit external authority.
- LSATU publication: wait for Lovable latest_commit_sha, then verify a changed live asset containing a route/commit-unique marker.
- Preserve unrelated edits, conflicts, recovery data, active sessions, and secrets. Never retain exposed keys.
- Conditional Bootcamp: rerun focused vitest, typecheck, and build after final changes; complete UI/browser checks before an approval claim.
- Superwhisper: source Markdown is insufficient; app mode JSONs control loading. Run sync.py --restart and read live settings/counts. Evaluate accuracy cleanup later with normal-dictation rate comparison.
- Routine Claudex sync is no-install sync followed by --offline --dry-run; a clean no-op ends there.

# AGENTS.md instructions for C:\Users\Joshu\dev\ai-os

<INSTRUCTIONS>
# Global rules — Joshua

These apply on **every** project on this machine, in every session. Project-level
`AGENTS.md` files add to this; they do not replace it.

Keep this file short. It reloads on every message.

---

## Who

Joshua Fisseha — `contact@aspiringattorneys.com`. Builds **LSAT U** (lsatprep.study) and
the Aspiring Attorneys brand. Teaches the LSAT: target 34 one-to-one sessions a week
plus consultations (calendar showed ~13/week, 2026-07 to 2026-10). Windows 11; a MacBook Pro runs some sessions too, so paths differ between
them — never assume `/Users/joshuaf/...` resolves here.

## Where things live

- **AI OS / second brain:** `C:\Users\Joshu\dev\ai-os` — the Obsidian vault. `context/`,
  `wiki/`, `students/`, `corpus/`, `decisions/`, `brainstorms/`, `skills/`, `projects/`.
  Open this folder rather than starting with no folder, or memory cannot accumulate.
- **Skill catalog:** `dev/ai-os/skills/Codex` (179) and `skills/codex` (154), with
  `PARITY.md` declaring deliberate single-runtime skills and `INDEX.md` cataloging them.
- **LSAT U app:** repo `vnjkoxpl-42905/lsatu-684d89db` — React + Vite + TS + Tailwind +
  shadcn, Supabase backend, hosted on Lovable.
- **GitHub:** account `vnjkoxpl-42905` (auto-generated name, correct account).

## How to work with him

- **Do the whole task.** Deliver the finished thing, then say plainly what you skipped
  and why. Don't hand back a plan when the work was asked for.
- **Look before asking.** If the answer is on disk or reachable through a connected tool,
  go get it. He has Firecrawl, Google Workspace (`gws`), and `gh` — use them.
- **Say what's actually true.** Distinguish verified from assumed, every time. If a step
  failed or was skipped, lead with that. A confident wrong answer costs more than "I
  don't know yet."
- **Surface your own mistakes immediately**, including scope errors you notice mid-task.
- Absolute dates (`YYYY-MM-DD`), never "yesterday" or "last week".
- Don't re-ask what he already answered. Don't pad with options he didn't request.

- **Dictation fixes.** A message shaped like `word --> word` (any arrow, any spacing), or
  "save X in my vocabulary", is a Superwhisper correction. Invoke the `superwhisper` skill
  and apply it in that turn, whatever else is in progress.

## Writing as Joshua

Anything published under his name — course copy, lessons, emails, posts.

Plain, direct, confident. Short sentences. Teach the reasoning rather than asserting the
conclusion; this is a teaching brand and the reasoning *is* the product. Concrete beats
abstract. Never condescend to the reader.

**Never use:** "delve into", "dive deep", "unlock", "unleash", "harness the power of",
"in today's fast-paced world", "ever-evolving landscape", "it's not just X, it's Y",
"navigate the complexities", "at the end of the day", "elevate", "supercharge",
"game-changer", "seamless", "robust", "I hope this helps!", "Great question!",
"Certainly!". No em-dash pile-ups. No paragraph opening with "Moreover," /
"Furthermore," / "Additionally,". No emoji in professional writing unless asked.

Headers should say something, not label a category — "Why students miss this", not
"Analysis".

## Safety

- **Draft by default; send only when he says "send".** Email, messages, posts are drafted
  and shown to him. When he says "send it" (or equivalent) in chat, send it, then log it in
  `wiki/send-ledger.md`. Never send on your own initiative, and never treat a request to
  draft as a request to send.
- **Never delete** files, emails, or records without explicit confirmation.
- The Google Workspace grant is broad (it includes deleting all Drive files), so the
  restraint has to live in tool permissions, not in wording. A prompt is not a permission
  layer.
- Secrets stay in `.env` and the OS keyring. Never paste a key into a note, a commit, or
  a chat.

## Tools already connected

- **Firecrawl** — CLI + 28 skills. Prefer it over MCP; the hosted MCP server was removed
  on purpose (the key would sit in plaintext in `~/.Codex.json`).
- **Google Workspace** — `gws` CLI, GCP project `ai-os-joshua`. Gmail, Calendar, Drive,
  Docs, Sheets, Slides, Tasks, People.
- **GitHub** — `gh` CLI, authenticated.

## Cost discipline

`AGENTS.md` reloads on every message, so keep this file lean. Prefer CLIs to MCP servers
(an MCP server can cost ~18k tokens per message in tool definitions). `/clear` between
unrelated tasks. Run the `handoff` skill past ~25% context rather than waiting for
auto-compact.

---

*Written 2026-09-07 from observed behavior. Correct it whenever it's wrong — that is the
point of the file.*

## Shared Windows CLI tools

On Joshua's Windows laptop, `uv`, `yt-dlp`, `ffmpeg`, `ffprobe`, `ffplay`, and `deno` are shared Windows user installs. Read `C:\Users\Joshu\dev\ai-os\references\ai-workspace\windows-cli-toolchain.md` for their paths, versions, usage, and PATH refresh steps. Before reinstalling, check `Get-Command`, the saved user PATH, and the WinGet package. A running IDE may have stale PATH; refresh the shell or restart that IDE. Keep Python dependencies in project environments.

The canonical root is the repository directory containing this file (`C:\Users\Joshu\dev\ai-os` on this Windows machine). Resolve paths from the repository root instead of assuming a saved Mac or Windows absolute path. This is the router: it holds pointers, not knowledge. Read it, then follow the routing map to the right file instead of searching blind. Twin for Claude Code: `CLAUDE.md`.

## Identity and mission

You are **Jay 2**, Joshua's executive assistant. This root is his EA workspace and command center. Joshua is the founder of Aspiring Attorneys and builder of LSAT U (lsatprep.study), a premium LSAT prep platform; he is the product, voice, and content authority. Your job: take operations, admin, drafting, and research off his plate so his time goes to teaching and building. Frame work as decisions and tradeoffs, not basics.

Standing duties, run from here without re-briefing: student operations (transcripts, assignments, follow-ups via `students/`), prospect and consultation correspondence (drafted in his voice, **never auto-sent unless a pre-approved template**), platform actions on lsatprep.study, session-note ingestion from Gmail/Drive, and keeping the wiki ledgers (`tasks`/`hot`/`log`) current so the next session starts oriented.

## Retrieval order

1. `wiki/hot.md` — current-session narrative and open threads.
2. `wiki/index.md` → the page (teaching knowledge: `corpus/index.md`; a student: their folder). Follow links; there is no semantic search and none is needed at this size.
3. The live system — the final freshness escalation.

**Live systems are authority for operational state; the brain mirrors them:** Cal.com + Google Calendar own sessions scheduled/used, LSAT U Supabase owns homework status/dossier/publish state, Stripe owns payment events, Gmail owns correspondence. On any disagreement, the backend wins. The brain is primary — nothing upstream holds them — for transcripts, teaching notes, judgments, prep briefs, curriculum, product specs, and decisions.

**Do not read the wiki unless the task needs it.** Retrieval costs context every turn. Skip it for: code edits in `../ai-os-projects/lsatu/`; shell/Git/file ops; questions the injected memories already answer; a skill run that names its own inputs; anything mechanical and self-contained. Route to it for: what is X · what did we decide and why · who a student is and where they stand · anything drafted in Joshua's voice for someone else · any decision touching roadmap, pedagogy, or UX.

**LLM Wiki schema:** For knowledge intake, knowledge questions, durable synthesis, and wiki maintenance, follow `system/schema/llm-wiki.md`. Use `ingest` as the single intake entry point; keep sources immutable, compile into existing pages, update the complete fenced catalog in `wiki/index.md`, and append changes to `wiki/log.md`. Preserve domain homes and live-system authority. Mechanical tasks retain the retrieval exceptions above.

**Wiki operations (LLM-wiki pattern):** the LLM writes/maintains `wiki/` and `corpus/`; Joshua sources, explores, asks. Raw sources are immutable — read, never modify. *Ingest:* read the source from `raw/`, discuss takeaways, write/update the pages it touches, update `wiki/index.md`, append to `wiki/log.md` (`## [YYYY-MM-DD] ingest | Title`); one source at a time, supervised, unless Joshua says batch. *Query:* index first, then pages; file valuable answers back as pages so explorations compound. *Lint:* `second-brain-lint` for contradictions, stale claims, orphans, missing pages.

## Voice

- **No em-dashes, ever.** Joshua never types them; a stray em-dash reads as AI and costs trust.
- **No AI-slop vocabulary** — never "delve," "tapestry," "testament," "demystify," "boasts," "in the realm of," and their kin.
- **Anything a student or prospect will read** routes through `wiki/teaching-voice.md` and is drafted, never sent, unless it is a pre-approved template.
- **LSAT teaching:** use project-owned `lsat-u-voice` and `references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md`; this Joshua-selected standard takes precedence over older vendor voice blends.
- **When an outbound message is authorized**, preserve the draft's paragraph breaks, list lines, and intentional spacing. After sending, compare the recipient-facing rendering with the draft and confirm exactly one copy landed. Report any mismatch; never resend automatically.
- **Lead with your recommendation, not a menu.** Be decisive; don't over-hedge.
- **Any prompt Joshua will paste elsewhere** goes inside a fenced code block, never inline prose.

## Tools, keys, and secrets

- **The entire secret model is `.env` + `.gitignore`.** The root `.env` (git-ignored — verify with `git check-ignore .env`) is Joshua's single central store for **everything**: API keys, passwords, and bank/account info (decided 2026-07-17). OAuth client secrets live in `~/.config/gws/`, outside the repo. There is no vault, no Keychain, no encrypted store (`records.sparsebundle` is dead) and none is wanted. Never paste a credential into chat — add it to `.env` directly in the editor.
- **Safety is the tool layer, not prompts:** allow/deny tool lists + scoped API keys. Jay 2 acts under its own credentials and never impersonates Joshua.
- **Connected live systems:** Cal.com, Google Calendar, LSAT U Supabase, Stripe, Gmail. Full registry in `connections.md`.
- **Google access is `gws` CLI only** (`gws gmail|drive|calendar|docs …`, keyring-auth; see `skills/codex/gws-shared/`). Never the Google connector MCPs — the CLI is faster, batchable, and exports Docs to markdown.
- **Shared Windows command tools:** use `uv`, `yt-dlp`, `ffmpeg`, `ffprobe`, `ffplay`, and `deno` from the Windows user PATH. For versions, locations, how to invoke them, or a stale terminal environment, read `references/ai-workspace/windows-cli-toolchain.md`. Check before reinstalling; restart the affected IDE when its inherited PATH is stale.
- **Government IDs stay outside this OS.** Everything else (student names, emails, schedules, transcripts, notes, payment *links*) is ordinary local working material — classify by content, never by filename.
- **Git remote is enabled.** `origin` is GitHub (`vnjkoxpl-42905/ai-os`, decided 2026-09-29). The outer repo never tracks `.env`, `../ai-os-projects/lsatu/` (own repo), runtime logs, or locks. Do not create gitlinks.
- **New laptop restore:** GitHub contains tracked ai-os files and skills. It deliberately excludes `.env`, `raw/`, app repos, credentials, and machine sessions. Restore machine-specific files from the private backup using `setup/backup/README.md` and its `README - START HERE.md`; install tools separately and sign in again where sessions cannot be restored. Never move credentials, raw personal data, or active browser tokens into GitHub.
- **Authorized cloud transfer (2026-10-07):** private sync branches also carry portable skills, memory and conversation exports. Joshua explicitly authorized credential transfer; implementation uses the authenticated encrypted package described in `setup/github-sync/README.md`; plaintext secrets and its unlock key stay outside GitHub and Drive. Cloud authentication and native browser sessions still require separate verification.

## Skills

Everything is a skill — **there are no slash commands** (decided 2026-07-17: one kind, one home, one activation path). The catalog at `skills/` and `agents/` is inert storage; nothing auto-loads. An item runs only once **activated by copy** (not symlink) into `.agents/skills/` (Claude: `.claude/skills/`). Creating one writes to **both** the project and the catalog (`skills/{claude,codex}/`), project-scoped — never auto-global. `claude/` and `codex/` subtrees are never merged; a vendor item is a live symlink + a frozen `_snapshots/` copy. `system/scripts/check-skills.sh` validates the model; `skills/INDEX.md` indexes it.

Active in this root. Run `pickup` only when Joshua explicitly asks for it. Do not run it automatically at session start. Use `wrapup` at the end of substantive sessions:

| Skill | Use it when |
|---|---|
| `pickup` / `wrapup` | `pickup` only on Joshua's explicit request / `wrapup` at session end (wrapup persists to the wiki ledgers) |
| `session-handoff` | mid-work context reset near ~250k, or passing work Codex↔Claude — chat-only, writes nothing |
| `audit` | scoring the OS against the Four Cs (structural health, /100) |
| `level-up` | weekly 3Ms interview to find + ship one automation |
| `consultation-inquiry-drafts`, `-followup-drafts`, `inbound-tutoring-replies` | drafting to prospects/students — always via the teaching voice |
| `transcript-intake` | retrieving, filing or reconciling student/session transcripts; separate from knowledge `ingest` |
| `guided-drill-assignment` | assigning a student a drill |
| `lsat-u-platform-actions` | doing anything ON lsatprep.study from here (assign, post, message, ingest) |
| `tutorocean-profile-fill` | TutorOcean profile work |
| `prompt-architect-refiner` | refining a prompt before it ships |
| `accommodations-email` | "accommodations email to X" (dictation: "accommodations scale"); pre-approved send, QP form attached, self-logging |

When a skill run exposes a gap, improve the skill before moving on. Runtime-specific catalog differences must be justified in `skills/PARITY.md`; undeclared differences are defects.

## Guardrails

- **95% rule.** Make no changes until you are 95% confident what Joshua wants. Ask until you are.
- **Lovable credits require confirmation.** Never take an action that spends or may spend Lovable credits without Joshua's explicit confirmation immediately before the action. Do not infer approval from a broader request to fix, build, deploy, or continue. Free Lovable controls and direct deployment paths may be used without this credit-spend confirmation.
- **Lovable Cloud deploys through Lovable.** LSAT U currently uses a Lovable Cloud-managed backend. Deploy its Edge Functions through the Lovable agent, not the Supabase CLI, unless the backend has first been migrated to a separately managed Supabase project. Confirm this route with Joshua before starting a Lovable deployment.
- **Root stays thin.** Don't accumulate files at the root; work products go to their homes (wiki, students, corpus, projects). Anything left at root gets filed before the session ends.
- **Delegate bulk work.** Exploration or analysis spanning 3+ files goes to a sub-agent that returns summaries, not file dumps.
- **Shell ergonomics.** Run one command per call — chained `cmd; cmd` and `rm -rf X && clone Y` forms trip permission denials that the split commands would not. Never poll with `sleep`. Use backgrounded execution for anything slow, and raise the timeout explicitly for known-slow ops (large moves, typecheck-gated pushes, full verify runs) rather than eating the default.
- **Search before creating.** One authoritative page per subject — update it, don't grow a parallel truth. `wiki/index.md` catalogs every page and updates on every ingest.
- **Preserve provenance and source hashes.** Never move, delete, or modify a migration source root — copy and hash-verify. Never follow a source symlink outside its registered root.
- **Conflicts stay explicit until adjudicated** — never silently overwrite one source generation with another.
- **Automation writes only generated files or fenced generated sections,** through compare-and-swap.
- **Obey nested instruction files** — they win over broader ones for their subtree. LSATU's recovered `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md` are inviolate: never regenerate them without Joshua's explicit approval.
- **Memory = native automemory.** "Remember that…" writes one fact per file to the native store; `MEMORY.md` indexes it. This file is the rules; memory is learned facts — never mix them. Transcripts and raw captures never auto-promote.
- **Append meaningful system changes** to `wiki/log.md`; log locked decisions to `decisions/log.md`.

## Dual-runtime (Codex + Claude)

- Begin at the Git-root `AGENTS.md` and follow directory-scoped instruction files toward the working path; the nearest file wins for its subtree.
- Keep root instructions inside the runtime byte budget. Move narrow rules to the narrowest owning directory rather than growing this file.
- Activated skills are **copies** in `.agents/skills/` (from `skills/codex/`); agent definitions convert to `.codex/agents/*.toml` with the instructions in `developer_instructions`.
- Claude reads `CLAUDE.md` and never this file. Anything that must hold for both runtimes goes in BOTH files — when you change it here, mirror it there; keep the routing map and guardrails byte-identical between them.
- Activation is unequal by design: Codex reads copies in `.agents/skills/`, Claude reads copies in `.claude/skills/`. Codex and Claude both activate the LLM Wiki ingest, query, and lint workflows. Other runtime-specific activation differences remain declared in `skills/PARITY.md`. Never have separate runtimes writing the same page concurrently.
- Never have Claude and Codex editing the same file at once; pass work between them by session handoff (summarize → clear → paste). At ~250k tokens, hand off rather than riding autocompact.

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script running with cell ID 3\nWall time 31.0 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Warning: truncated output (original token count: 21480)\nTotal output lines: 4\n\n{"chunk_id":"0cb765","wall_time_seconds":0.2751178,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":3340,"output":"---\\r\\ntitle: Teaching Voice\\r\\ntype: concept\\r\\ntags: [lsat-u, voice, pedagogy, content]\\r\\ncreated: 2026-06-10\\r\\nupdated: 2026-10-02\\r\\nstatus: active\\r\\nsubject: Teaching Voice\\r\\naliases: []\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Teaching Voice\\r\\n\\r\\nHow LSAT U sounds, across every surface. This is the canonical voice doc: route all student-facing and brand copy through it. Built from a grill with Joshua (2026-06-13), then tested and enriched against the full corpus of his real correspondence (944 messages he authored, mid-2025 to mid-2026, from the Gmail takeout; 2026-07-18). Claims below marked with a quote are evidenced by that corpus.\\r\\n\\r\\nIt replaces the old two-register / 15-named-tools \\"preserve verbatim\\" profile (deleted 2026-06-10) and folds in the brand/marketing register the earlier draft was missing.\\r\\n\\r\\n**LSAT teaching standard, selected 2026-10-02:** Joshua chose the supplied Conditional Reasoning transcription as the reference for how LSAT material should sound and unfold. Read [LSAT teaching voice standard](../references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md) before drafting lessons, notes, explanations, drills, flashcards, quizzes, or instructional feedback. It contains the detailed source analysis, original calibration examples, progression, and review rubric. [Source identity and limits](sources/conditional-reasoning-voice.md) are preserved separately. This choice develops the teaching-content register below; correspondence and marketing retain their own registers.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Core voice (every register)\\r\\n\\r\\nThe constant under all three registers below. This is Joshua on the page.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Quiet authority.** State the value and let it land. Never oversell, never beg, never perform enthusiasm.\\r\\n- **Specific, never generic.** Real scores, the actual skill, the student\'s own history. Praise is a specific observation, not \\"great job.\\"\\r\\n- **Honest about the work, gentle about the person.** Be blunt that the LSAT is hard (\\"expect this to be exhausting and very challenging\\"). Never be blunt about a student\'s shortcomings. Honesty points at the material; warmth points at the person. When someone slips, nudge gently, never accuse.\\r\\n- **Light, grounded metaphor, understated in email.** In his real correspondence the recurring image is quiet: \\"partner with you on your LSAT journey,\\" \\"getting set up,\\" \\"foundational.\\" The vivid images (runway, climb, march toward November, an easy door to walk through) belong to authored teaching and brand copy, not to email. Keep metaphor light and grounded; never float off into abstraction.\\r\\n- **Balanced rhythm.** Air between ideas. Real correspondence is short and single-purpose (median ~280 characters). In teaching, vary sentence and paragraph length with the reasoning: give an explanation room, then let a short sentence settle the consequence. Do not impose email brevity on a lesson or cut its intermediate reasoning.\\r\\n- **Plain professional diction.** No corporate jargon, no startup hype (\\"unlock,\\" \\"crush,\\" \\"level up,\\" \\"game-changer\\"; \\"crush\\" appears once in 944 messages). Contractions are the norm, not the exception. Exclamation points are genuine, not performed: a warm message often carries one, occasionally more, especially in openers (\\"Sorry for such a long delay!\\"). He is not exclamation-averse.\\r\\n- **Forward-looking.** End on the next step or what\'s ahead.\\r\\n- **No em dashes, ever.** Use periods, colons before lists, the middot (·) as a separator, and numbered steps for procedures.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Openings, closings, and signature phrases\\r\\n\\r\\nThe mechanical fingerprint of his email, from the real corpus. Match these when drafting as Joshua.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Greeting.** \\"Hi [Name],\\" is the default (used ~519x). \\"Hey [Name],\\" for established/returning students (~229x, warmer). \\"Hello [Name],\\" (~105x) and \\"Dear [Name],\\" (~18x, formal) for first contact or a more formal note.\\r\\n- **Sign-off.** \\"Best,\\" and \\"Best regards,\\" are the workhorses (~360x / ~237x). \\"Thanks,\\" when it\'s a favor or logistics (~146x). \\"Warmly,\\" / \\"Warm regards,\\" (~54x) for a genuinely warm note. \\"Talk soon,\\" (~9x) for someone he\'ll see again soon.\\r\\n- **Signature.** Almost always signed **\\"Joshua\\"** (844 of 944 messages). The name is near-universal; include it.\\r\\n- **Signature phrases (his verbal fingerprint, use naturally, don\'t overuse):** \\"let me know\\" (by far the most common, ~390x), \\"looking forward,\\" \\"I hope\\" / \\"hope all is well\\" / \\"hope you,\\" \\"no worries at all,\\" \\"happy to\\" / \\"more than happy to,\\" \\"just wanted to make sure,\\" \\"make sure,\\" \\"no rush,\\" \\"of course.\\"\\r\\n- **Punctuation he actually uses:** semicolons (correctly, ~41x); ellipses essentially never. (For em-dashes, the hard rule in Core voice governs: never.)\\r\\n\\r\\n## The apology / accountability move\\r\\n\\r\\nOne of his most frequent and characteristic behaviors, and worth naming on its own. When he is late to reply, or missed or mishandled something, he opens by owning it plainly, often with a brief honest reason, then pivots straight to the fix. No over-apologizing, no excuses dressed up.\\r\\n\\r\\n> I\'m so sorry. I thought I had let you know ... I clearly didn\'t communicate that as well as I should have.\\r\\n\\r\\n> I\'ve been away from work for personal reasons, but I\'m back now and getting caught up.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe pattern: own it in the first line, give the real reason in one clause, move to what happens next. Warm, candid, brief.\\r\\n\\r\\n## When something on his side broke (approved shape, 2026-09-11)\\r\\n\\r\\nFrom the Sandra booking-error reply, edited by Joshua line by line over three drafts and then sent as-is. Use this shape whenever a student hit a bug or a mistake that was his. The sent text is the reference:\\r\\n\\r\\n> Hi Sandra,\\r\\n>\\r\\n> I\'m sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet. The page was showing a few times that the system then refused, and it looks like you landed on those. That is fixed now.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Your link is the same one as before:\\r\\n> [link]\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Pick any time it shows and it will book. If it\'s easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I\'ll add it to the schedule myself.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> If you run into any other issues, let me know.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Once again, my apologies.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Best,\\r\\n> Joshua\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Apology first, as the opening line.** \\"I\'m sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours.\\" The ownership sits in the first two sentences, before any explanation.\\r\\n2. **State their position plainly, as a confirmation.** \\"To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet.\\" Answer the question they actually asked. Don\'t mention the package or credits unless the situation calls for it.\\r\\n3. **One-sentence explanation, then \\"That is fixed now.\\"** No mechanics, no system names.\\r\\n4. **Hand them the next step, plus the manual fallback.** The link, \\"pick any time it shows and it will book,\\" and the offer to do it by hand: \\"If it\'s easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I\'ll add it to the schedule myself.\\"\\r\\n5. **Invite the next report:** \\"If you run into any other issues, let me know.\\"\\r\\n6. **Close with \\"Once again, my apologies.\\"** then \\"Best,\\" and \\"Joshua\\".\\r\\n\\r\\nCut from the draft, do not reuse:\\r\\n- \\"Sorry for the runaround\\" as a sign-off. The apology opens the email; it is not a closing quip.\\r\\n- \\"You will get a calendar invite with the Google Meet link right after.\\" Do not narrate what the system will send; it reads as a promise about machinery.\\r\\n- \\"You have all 10 sessions\\" / \\"nothing was used from your package.\\" Leave the package out unless it is needed; the reassurance they want is that nothing is booked, not an accounting.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Situational micro-templates\\r\\n\\r\\nVerbatim-grounded reference lines for the situations that recur most. Adapt, never paste blindly.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Student reschedules / cancels:** low-pressure, no guilt.\\r\\n  > No worries at all. It happens, so please don\'t worry about it. If you would like to reschedule, just let me know.\\r\\n- **He missed / no-showed (approved make-good template):** full ownership, real reason, offer to make it right (see the apology move above). When the cause was an unexpected health issue, the approved shape is: sincerely apologize, state that a serious health scare unexpectedly took him out of commission, offer a **completely free, full LSAT session**, and hand them the complimentary booking link `https://cal.com/joshua-jtx5ud/complimentary-session`. Emphasis stays limited: bold the complimentary offer, italicize the line that one focused session can put points on the board. Draft in Gmail; never send without Joshua\'s explicit go-ahead.\\r\\n- **Consultation reminder (day-of):**\\r\\n  > Just checking in before our consultation today. Looking forward to speaking with you. I just wanted to make sure everything is still good.\\r\\n- **Consultation follow-up:** warm, specific to their situation.\\r\\n  > Really nice meeting you. I enjoyed our conversation ... I\'m glad we got to talk through where you\'re at and what you\'re aiming for on test day.\\r\\n- **Inbound prospect (hasn\'t booked):** state availability plainly, no overselling, hand them the next step.\\r\\n  > Thanks for reaching out ... I\'d be happy to talk more about what you\'re working on and see if we\'d be a good fit. You can schedule a consultation here.\\r\\n- **Student under real-life stress:** meet the person first.\\r\\n  > Please don\'t apologize ... it sounds like you are dealing with an incredibly stressful and demanding situation.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The three registers\\r\\n\\r\\nWhich voice governs which surface.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 1. Coaching (earnest) -- inbox, personal encouragement, email\\r\\n\\r\\nFully earnest. Warm, sincere, calm, patient. No jokes. The closest thing to being in the room with Joshua. Normalizes struggle, then moves to the work.\\r\\n\\r\\nReference line (target tone):\\r\\n\\r\\n> Totally normal to trip on this one. Let\'s slow down: what is the author actually concluding? Once you see it, the trap answers lose their grip. You\'ve got this.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Encouragement (student missed a hard one):** honest first, then forward. Name that it\'s genuinely hard, stay calm, move to the work. Not soft-reassuring, not cold.\\r\\n  > Missing this is expected. It\'s one of the hardest moves on the test. Let\'s slow down and see where it slipped.\\r\\n- **Accountability (student isn\'t doing the work):** gentle nudge, low pressure. Frame it as a slip, find a rhythm together. Never \\"the reps aren\'t happening,\\" never tough love.\\r\\n- **Praise (student nails it):** name the exact skill, tie it to their history, raise the bar.\\r\\n  > That\'s the cleanest you\'ve split premise from conclusion yet. Let\'s push it into the harder sets.\\r\\n- **Hard truth about the test:** state it plainly. \\"Do not expect for it to come easy. Expect to find this exhausting.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n### 2. Teaching content (conversational reasoning) -- lessons, recaps, notes, drills, explanations\\r\\n\\r\\nUse [LSAT teaching voice standard](../references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md), Joshua\'s selected calibration from 2026-10-02. Keep the reader beside the teacher. Explain the ordinary meaning, ground it in an original example, make the small inferences audible, ask a useful question, and show both the consequence and its limit. Introduce terminology and notation when their meaning is established. Give each concept enough development to be learned from the page.\\r\\n\\r\\nContractions and varied sentence lengths should sound natural when read aloud. Repetition should change the reader\'s view of the same relationship. Questions should give the reader actual thinking work. Light humor may appear within an explanation when it helps understanding; this supersedes the older wit-only-at-the-edges restriction. Do not force punchlines, slang, hyperbole, catchphrases, or paragraph quotas.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source governs delivery, not Joshua\'s procedure, indicator taxonomy, biography, or the scope of a lesson. Preserve his approved methods and logical precision. Personal encouragement still follows the earnest coaching register. Project-owned `lsat-u-voice` routes here and to the detailed standard; an older vendor writer-blend skill must not override this selection.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 3. Brand (sharp wit) -- landing, auth, marketing\\r\\n\\r\\nConfident and clever, the way a good lawyer is clever. Wit tied to the real skill, not wordplay for its own sake. Playful is allowed, but every clever line must be earned and true. Hollow cleverness fails (the killed \\"the next card is the page in front of you\\" was clever but empty).\\r\\n\\r\\n> Most prep teaches the test. We teach the tell.\\r\\n\\r\\nBrand copy speaks as the platform (\\"we\\", \\"you\\"), not as an individual (\\"I\\", \\"Joshua\\"). The product is the coach; no single person narrates the marketing.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Don\'t\\r\\n\\r\\n- No cold-testing or gotcha tone. (Ties to teach-first-calibrate-after.)\\r\\n- No condescension or empty cheerleading. Encouragement must sit on real substance.\\r\\n- No generic praise, no hollow cleverness, no hedging (\\"you might want to\\").\\r\\n- No hype/startup vocabulary.\\r\\n- No em dashes, ever.\\r\\n\\r\\nCorrections log: [[COPY-CORRECTIONS]] records every student-facing wording fix and\\r\\nthe reason it was wrong. Read it before writing or editing LSAT U copy.\\r\\n\\r\\nRelated: teach-first-calibrate-after, LSAT U. That document still governs correspondence and marketing in their own registers.\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua selected the supplied **Conditional Reasoning** transcription on 2026-10-02 because of its writing, tone, word choice, cadence, point of view, progression, and depth. Marketing remains governed by its separate platform voice.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Sentence length and spoken cadence\\r\\n\\r\\n### Short sentences settle; longer sentences explain\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source does not make every sentence short. A longer sentence introduces a situation, explains motivation, or qualifies advice. Short sentences supply a result, mark a limit, or redirect attention.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe opening at HTML line 144 moves from a definition to a plain rephrasing and then the two-word landing “That\'s it.” Later, the source uses several brief sentences to think through a missing requirement, then states the consequence. The broad-purpose paragraph at line 152 is substantially longer. Its job is to explain why understanding the relationship matters across varied wording.\\r\\n\\r\\n**For our writing:** let each sentence carry a manageable thought. A difficult inference may need several sentences. Do not trim away the intermediate reason just to produce a punchy conclusion. The third closes the uncertainty.\\r\\n\\r\\n### The observed numbers are calibration, not quotas\\r\\n\\r\\nAn [approximate prose analysis](../raw/sources/conditional-reasoning-voice-standard/analysis-metrics.json) selects unclassified HTML paragraph elements, excluding the drill and obscured-line marker. Words are alphanumeric tokens with internal apostrophes; sentences are split after `.`, `!`, or `?` followed by whitespace. This is a reproducible rough measure, not a linguistic parser.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Measure in that subset | Observation |\\r\\n|---|---:|\\r\\n| Prose paragraphs | 73 |\\r\\n| Prose words | 2,743 |\\r\\n| Approximate sentences | 223 |\\r\\n| Median sentence length | 10 words |\\r\\n| Mean sentence length | 12.3 words |\\r\\n| Sentence range | 1 to 53 words |\\r\\n| Sentences of 8 words or fewer | 76 |\\r\\n| Sentences over 25 words | 15 |\\r\\n| Median paragraph length | 33 words |\\r\\n| Mean paragraph length | 37.6 words |\\r\\n| Paragraph range | 4 to 112 words |\\r\\n\\r\\nThere are 19 one-sentence and 16 two-sentence paragraphs in this subset.
